To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the aorta dilates during the development of hypertension, that dilation of the aortic lumen is due to a combination of both pulsatile and diastolic dilation and that dilation occurs at a time that is consistent with the time course required for complete resetting of the aortic baroreceptor.

the dilation of the aortic arch is a gradual process that takes place in two phases, the first phase (6-24 h) being associated with a marked increase of both dynamic and mean distensibility of aortic wall and the second phase (24-48 h) being accompanied only by a gradual increase in pulsation caliber with no change of mean distensibility.
the time course of the development of hypertension in rats is associated with a gradual dilation of the aortic lumen, which reaches its maximal level after 48 h.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role played by the aortic wall in the development of sustained arterial hypertension.

the development of an aortic pressure transducer that can be used to monitor, for a prolonged period of time, changes in both pressure and caliber of the aortic lumen in freely moving rats with experimental hypertension.

the development and application of an implantable strain gauge for the measurement of arterial caliber and mechanical properties in the conscious, unrestrained rat and the application of this method for studying the changes in arterial wall properties during the development and maintenance of hypertension.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
during the development of hypertension the aorta undergoes a dilation that is accompanied by a marked change in its mechanical properties.
the aortic dilation and increased distensibility during the development of hypertension may be the consequence of the resetting of the aortic baroreceptor system.
dilation of the aortic caliber is an integral component of the development of hypertension.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the aorta is capable of undergoing a significant degree of remodeling to accommodate the increase in pressure during the development of hypertension.

during the development of hypertension, the aorta undergoes an initial dilation, which is then followed by an increase in distensibility and a gradual return to the original resting diastolic caliber.
the resetting of aortic mechanoreceptors is a complex process involving both a change of the aortic caliber and the mechanical properties of the vessel wall.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the aorta is a dynamic structure and that the geometry of the vessel is an important determinant of its function.

aortic baroreceptor resetting is not simply a result of the change in the mechanical properties of the vessel wall, but it is a complex process that involves the interaction of several factors, such as aortic wall properties and the central nervous system.
the aortic wall dilates during the development of hypertension, and the dilation is accompanied by a significant increase in the dynamic distensiblity of the aortic walls.
